claim: 227 patients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection and meeting ARDS criteria were included in the study from March 16, 2020 to December 10, 2020.
source: All patients with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (Escudero et al., 2020) and meeting the Kigali modification (Riviello et al., 2016) of ARDS criteria (to include patients without mechanical ventilation) from March 16, 2020 to December 10, 2020 were included in the study.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of patients, inclusion criteria, and study period with supporting citations.

claim: IFIH1 rs1990760 variants in the study population met Hardy-Weinberg conditions (53 CC, 110 CT, 64 TT, chi-square p=0.19).
source: IFIH1 rs1990760 variants in this population met Hardy-Weinberg conditions (53 CC, 110 CT, 64 TT, chi-square p=0.19).
evidence: Statistical test results are provided showing the genotype distribution meets Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

claim: Patients with the IFIH1 rs1990760 TT variant showed lower PaO2/FiO2 ratio at admission compared to CC/CT variants.
source: There were no differences in comorbidities or clinical data at admission between genotypes other than a lower PaO2/FiO2 ratio in patients with a TT variant (Table 1).
evidence: Table 1 shows PaO2/FiO2 values with p=0.007, indicating statistically significant difference.

claim: Expression of IFIH1 was significantly lower in patients with the TT genotype compared to CC/CT genotypes.
source: Expression of IFIH1 was significantly lower in patients with the TT genotype (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 2A shows boxplots with p=0.019 comparing IFIH1 expression between genotypes.

claim: 179 genes showed significant differential expression between patients with TT and CT/CC variants.
source: Comparison of peripheral blood gene expression between patients with TT and CT/CC variants yielded significant differences in 179 genes (Figure 2B–C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript states the number of differentially expressed genes and references figures and supplementary data.

claim: Patients with the TT genotype showed an increase in hematopoietic precursors and myeloid dendritic cells compared to CC/CT genotypes.
source: Patients with the TT genotype showed an increase in hematopoietic precursors and myeloid dendritic cells (Figure 3).
evidence: Figure 3 shows cell population proportions with p-values indicating significant differences for these cell types.

claim: Patients with the TT genotype showed lower serum levels of IL-6, CXCL10, CXCL16, and CCL7 compared to CC/CT genotypes.
source: Patients with the TT genotype showed lower levels of pro-inflammatory mediators, including IL-6, CXCL10, CXCL16, and CCL7 (Figure 4).
evidence: Figure 4 displays cytokine concentrations with adjusted p-values showing significant differences for these mediators.

claim: Dexamethasone increased expression of FOXO3 and IL6 only in cells with the TT variant when exposed to poly I:C.
source: However, the steroid increased the expression of FOXO3 (Figure 5C) and IL6 (Figure 5D) only in cells with the TT variant.
evidence: Figure 5C and 5D show gene expression results from ex-vivo experiments with statistical significance indicated for TT variant.

claim: All patients with the IFIH1 rs1990760 TT variant not treated with steroids survived their ICU stay (hazard ratio: 2.49, 95% CI: 1.29–4.79).
source: All patients with the TT allele (n=14) who did not receive steroids were discharged alive (HR: 2.49 [1.29–4.79], p=0.012).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific hazard ratio with confidence intervals and p-value for ICU survival outcome.

claim: Patients with a TT variant treated with dexamethasone showed increased hospital mortality (HR: 2.19, 95% CI: 1.01–4.87).
source: Patients with the TT allele and treated with steroids showed a worse outcome (19 deaths in 50 patients, HR: 2.19 [1.01–4.87], p=0.05).
evidence: The manuscript provides hazard ratio with confidence intervals and p-value for hospital mortality outcome.

claim: There were no differences in viral load at diagnosis among IFIH1 variants or treatment groups.
source: There were no differences in these parameters related to IFIH1 variants or treatment groups.
evidence: Figure 6C shows viral load data with p=0.888, indicating no significant differences.

claim: There were no differences in viral clearance after peak value among IFIH1 variants or treatment groups.
source: There were no differences in these parameters related to IFIH1 variants or treatment groups.
evidence: Figure 6D shows viral clearance data with p=0.056, indicating no significant differences.

claim: IL-6 levels were higher in patients with the TT variant treated with steroids after 1 week of ICU admission.
source: However, IL-6 levels were higher in those with the TT variant and treated with steroids, in line with our ex-vivo findings.
evidence: Figure 6F shows serum IL-6 levels at day 7 with p=0.014 and pairwise comparisons.

claim: IFIH1 expression decreased in patients with rs1990760 CC/CT variants treated with steroids, but not in those with a TT variant.
source: IFIH1 expression decreased in patients with rs1990760 CC/CT variants treated with steroids, but not in those with a TT variant (Figure 6G).
evidence: Figure 6G shows IFIH1 expression at ICU day 4 comparing steroid-treated and untreated patients by genotype.

claim: Steroids increased FOXO3 expression only in patients with a TT variant.
source: In opposite, steroids increased FOXO3 expression only in patients with a TT variant (Figure 6H), resembling the results from the ex-vivo experiments.
evidence: Figure 6H shows FOXO3 expression at ICU day 4 with p=0.02 for TT variant with dexamethasone.

claim: Steroids significantly changed the expression of 58 genes in patients with a CC/CT variant and 23 genes in patients with a TT variant.
source: When the whole transcriptomes were compared, steroids significantly changed the expression of 58 genes in patients with a CC/CT variant and 23 in patients with a TT variant (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers of differentially expressed genes with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Changes in gene expression induced by steroids were qualitatively different between variants, with only three genes in common.
source: Overall, changes in gene expression were qualitatively different between variants, with only three genes in common (Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 6I shows a Venn diagram illustrating the overlap of differentially expressed genes between variants.

claim: The T-allele frequency in populations from Black/Asian ancestry is 0.13.
source: The T-allele frequency in populations from a Black/Asian ancestry is 0.13 (data available at https://grasp.nhlbi.nih.gov/Covid19GWASResults.aspx), so only 1.7% has a TT variant.
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific database for allele frequency data.

claim: In Black/Asian populations, the risk ratio for dexamethasone treatment was 0.7 (0.51–0.95) in the RECOVERY trial.
source: In these populations, RR was 0.7 (0.51–0.95), whereas in patients from a White ancestry (with a T allele frequency of 0.61), RR increased to 0.9 (0.8–1.2).
evidence: The manuscript provides risk ratios with confidence intervals extracted from RECOVERY trial data.

claim: In White populations, the risk ratio for dexamethasone treatment was 0.9 (0.8–1.2) in the RECOVERY trial.
source: In these populations, RR was 0.7 (0.51–0.95), whereas in patients from a White ancestry (with a T allele frequency of 0.61), RR increased to 0.9 (0.8–1.2).
evidence: The manuscript provides risk ratios with confidence intervals extracted from RECOVERY trial data.

claim: The human gene IFIH1 encodes MDA5, a helicase that acts as a cytoplasmatic virus receptor.
source: The human gene IFIH1, located in the reverse strand of chromosome 2, encodes MDA5, a helicase that acts as a cytoplasmatic virus receptor.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about the IFIH1 gene and its protein product.

claim: After binding to viral RNA, MDA5 interacts with MAVS, triggering transcription of type-1 interferon genes and systemic inflammatory response.
source: After binding to a viral RNA strand, MDA5 interacts with a mitochondrial adapter (MAVS, mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein), triggering the transcription of type-1 interferon genes and ultimately the systemic inflammatory response.
evidence: This describes the established molecular mechanism of MDA5 signaling.

claim: The rs1990760 polymorphism encodes a variant of the IFIH1 gene (NM_022168: c.2836G > A [p.Ala946Thr]).
source: In humans, the rs1990760 polymorphism encodes a variant of the IFIH1 gene (NM_022168: c.2836G > A [p.Ala946Thr]) that has been related to different susceptibility to viral infections and autoimmune disorders (Gorman et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific genetic nomenclature and cites a reference for the association with disease susceptibility.

claim: In experimental models of Coxsackie virus infection, TT variants in rs1990760 result in lower pro-inflammatory cytokine levels without major reduction in viral clearance.
source: In experimental models of Coxsackie virus infection, TT variants in rs1990760 result in lower pro-inflammatory cytokine levels without a major reduction in viral clearance (Domsgen et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific study demonstrating this finding in an experimental model.

claim: Steroids and blockade of the IL-6 pathway are the only strategies that have decreased mortality in critically ill COVID-19 patients.
source: The only strategies that have decreased mortality in this population, steroids (WHO Rapid Evidence Appraisal for COVID-19 Therapies (REACT) Working Group et al., 2020) and blockade of the IL-6 pathway (REMAP-CAP Investigators et al., 2021), aim to limit this exacerbated immune response to prevent organ dysfunction.
evidence: The manuscript cites two major clinical trials supporting these therapeutic strategies.

claim: Mortality rates in critically ill COVID-19 patients remain around 27–32% despite treatment with steroids or IL-6 blockade.
source: However, mortality rates are still around 27–32% (REMAP-CAP Investigators et al., 2021; WHO Rapid Evidence Appraisal for COVID-19 Therapies (REACT) Working Group et al., 2020), so new therapeutic approaches are warranted.
evidence: The manuscript cites clinical trial data showing mortality rates despite current treatments.

claim: Pangolins lack functional IFIH1.
source: Notably, pangolins, an intermediate host of coronaviruses (Xiao et al., 2020), lack functional IFIH1.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this biological fact about pangolins.

claim: The absence of functional IFIH1 in pangolins has been suggested to reduce inflammatory response to coronavirus infections.
source: It has been suggested that this deficiency reduces the inflammatory response to coronavirus infections (Fischer et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference proposing this hypothesis about pangolins and coronavirus response.

claim: Long (high-molecular weight) poly-I:C binds specifically to MDA-5.
source: Although poly-I:C may bind to both RIG-I and MDA-5, long (high-molecular weight) poly-I:C binds specifically to MDA-5 (Kato et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting the specificity of high-molecular weight poly-I:C for MDA-5.

claim: The correlation coefficient between estimated and measured lymphocyte percentages was 0.61.
source: As a quality check, we analyzed the correlation between estimated and measured lymphocyte percentages. The obtained correlation coefficient was 0.61 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific correlation coefficient value with reference to a figure.

claim: In-silico predictions suggest that IFIH1 downregulation decreases the expression of pro-inflammatory pathways.
source: In-silico predictions suggest that IFIH1 downregulation (such as in patients with the rs1990760 TT variant) decreases the expression of pro-inflammatory pathways (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes computational modeling results shown in a figure.

claim: An in-silico analysis suggested that dexamethasone could disrupt some of the effects caused by IFIH1 downregulation.
source: An in-silico analysis focused on the interactions between IFIH1 and steroids suggested that dexamethasone could disrupt some of the effects caused by IFIH1 downregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes computational modeling results with reference to a figure.

claim: Dexamethasone may change expression of several IFIH1-dependent genes, including STAT1, STAT3, or FOXO3.
source: Specifically, dexamethasone may change expression of several IFIH1-dependent genes, including STAT1, STAT3, or FOXO3 among others.
evidence: This is based on in-silico analysis predictions described in the manuscript.

claim: Dexamethasone had no effect on STAT1 or STAT3 expression in PBMCs exposed to poly I:C.
source: Compared to exposure to poly I:C alone, dexamethasone had no effect on STAT1 (Figure 5A) or STAT3 (Figure 5B) expression.
evidence: Figure 5A and 5B show gene expression results from ex-vivo experiments.

claim: Median follow-up was 25 days (interquartile range 16–39 days) and 27 days in survivors (interquartile range 17–44 days).
source: Median follow-up was 25 days (interquartile range 16–39 days) and 27 days in survivors (interquartile range 17–44 days).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific follow-up duration data.

claim: In patients with CC/CT variants, dexamethasone was not related to better ICU survival outcome (98 out of 128 patients discharged, HR: 1.20 [0.78–1.38], p=0.41).
source: In patients with this variant, dexamethasone was not related to a better outcome (98 out of 128 patients discharged, HR: 1.20 [0.78–1.38], p=0.41).
evidence: The manuscript provides hazard ratio with confidence intervals and p-value for ICU survival outcome.

claim: Steroid treatment in patients with the TT variant was related to loss of survival benefit (32 out of 50 patients discharged alive, HR: 1.03 [0.62–1.72], p=0.91).
source: Steroid treatment in patients with the TT variant was related to the loss of this benefit (32 out of 50 patients discharged alive, HR: 1.03 [0.62–1.72], p=0.91).
evidence: The manuscript provides hazard ratio with confidence intervals and p-value for ICU survival outcome.

claim: All patients with the TT allele who were not treated with steroids survived after their hospital stay.
source: All patients with the TT allele who were not treated with steroids survived after their hospital stay (HR 1.23×10–7, confidence intervals, and p-value cannot be computed due to the absence of events).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states zero deaths in this group.

claim: Patients with CC/CT genotypes not treated with steroids had 9 hospital deaths out of 35 patients.
source: There were nine hospital deaths in patients with the CT/CC genotypes not treated with steroids (out of a total of 35 patients), and 27 out of 128 hospital deaths when treated with steroids, resulting in HR of 1.11 [0.52–2.37] (p=0.80).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific mortality counts and hazard ratio.

claim: Patients with CC/CT genotypes treated with steroids had 27 hospital deaths out of 128 patients (HR: 1.11 [0.52–2.37], p=0.80).
source: There were nine hospital deaths in patients with the CT/CC genotypes not treated with steroids (out of a total of 35 patients), and 27 out of 128 hospital deaths when treated with steroids, resulting in HR of 1.11 [0.52–2.37] (p=0.80).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific mortality counts and hazard ratio with confidence intervals.

claim: Patients with CC/CT variants and receiving dexamethasone showed lower levels of IL-6 at ICU admission compared to those not receiving steroids.
source: Compared to patients with CC/CT variants not treated with steroids, patients with the same genotype but receiving dexamethasone and patients with the TT variant not receiving steroids showed lower levels of IL-6 at admission (Figure 6E).
evidence: Figure 6E shows serum IL-6 concentrations at day 1 with p<0.001.

claim: Patients with the TT variant not receiving steroids showed lower levels of IL-6 at ICU admission compared to CC/CT variants not receiving steroids.
source: Compared to patients with CC/CT variants not treated with steroids, patients with the same genotype but receiving dexamethasone and patients with the TT variant not receiving steroids showed lower levels of IL-6 at admission (Figure 6E).
evidence: Figure 6E shows serum IL-6 concentrations at day 1 with p<0.001.

claim: After 1 week, serum IL-6 levels remained lower in patients receiving dexamethasone with the CC/CT variant.
source: After 1 week (Figure 6F), serum IL-6 levels remained lower in patients receiving dexamethasone with the CC/CT variant and in those with the TT variant and not treated with this drug.
evidence: Figure 6F shows serum IL-6 levels at day 7 with p=0.014.

claim: After 1 week, serum IL-6 levels remained lower in patients with the TT variant not treated with dexamethasone.
source: After 1 week (Figure 6F), serum IL-6 levels remained lower in patients receiving dexamethasone with the CC/CT variant and in those with the TT variant and not treated with this drug.
evidence: Figure 6F shows serum IL-6 levels at day 7 with p=0.014.

claim: Dexamethasone in mechanically ventilated patients in the RECOVERY trial had a hazard ratio of 0.64.
source: Dexamethasone in patients receiving mechanical ventilation at inclusion in the RECOVERY trial had an HR of 0.64, compared to an HR of 0.83 in the whole population.
evidence: The manuscript cites hazard ratios from the RECOVERY trial for different patient subgroups.

claim: The proportion of Black/Asian patients in the mechanically ventilated group of the RECOVERY trial was 29%.
source: Of note, the proportion of Black/Asian patients (with a low frequency of a T allele) in the mechanically ventilated group was 29%, but only 18% in the whole study population.
evidence: The manuscript provides demographic data from the RECOVERY trial.

claim: The proportion of Black/Asian patients in the whole RECOVERY trial population was 18%.
source: Of note, the proportion of Black/Asian patients (with a low frequency of a T allele) in the mechanically ventilated group was 29%, but only 18% in the whole study population.
evidence: The manuscript provides demographic data from the RECOVERY trial.

claim: The study was approved by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of Principado de Asturias (ref. 2020/188).
source: This single-center prospective, observational study was approved (ref. 2020/188) by the Clinical Research Ethics Committee of Principado de Asturias (Spain).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the ethics approval reference number.

claim: Informed consent was obtained from each participant or next of kin.
source: Informed consent was obtained from each participant or next of kin.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the consent process.

claim: The main outcome was intensive care unit discharge alive and spontaneously breathing.
source: The main outcome was intensive care unit (ICU) discharge alive and spontaneously breathing.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines the primary outcome measure.

claim: Secondary outcome was hospital discharge.
source: Secondary outcome was hospital discharge.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines the secondary outcome measure.

claim: All biochemical analyses were performed by researchers blinded to genotype and outcome.
source: All biochemical analyses (cytokine measurements, RNAseq, estimation of cell populations…, see below) were performed by researchers blinded to genotype and outcome.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the blinding procedure for laboratory analyses.

claim: Gene expression in peripheral blood was profiled in 42 patients who did not receive steroid therapy during the first day of ICU admission.
source: Gene expression in peripheral blood during the first day of ICU admission was profiled in 42 patients who did not receive steroid therapy at that time (11, 19, and 12 with rs1990760 TT, CT, and CC genotypes, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific sample sizes for the gene expression analysis.

claim: Serum cytokines were measured at ICU admission in 28 patients (8, 10, and 10 with TT, CT, and CC genotypes, respectively).
source: Serum cytokines were measured at ICU admission in 28 patients (8, 10, and 10 with TT, CT, and CC genotypes, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific sample sizes for cytokine measurements by genotype.

claim: There were no differences in any of the measured interferons between genotypes, which were below the limit of detection in a large proportion of patients.
source: There were no differences in any of the measured interferons, which were below the limit of detection in a large proportion of patients.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of differences and detection issues for interferons.

claim: There were no significant differences in any of the measured cytokines between patients with CC and CT variants.
source: There were no significant differences in any of the measured cytokines between patients with CC and CT variants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Blood samples for ex-vivo experiments were from healthy volunteers genotyped for IFIH1 rs1990760 variants (n=5, 6, and 7 for CC, CT, and TT variants, respectively).
source: To test these predictions, an ex-vivo experiment using PBMCs from healthy volunteers with different IFIH1 rs1990760 variants (n=5, 6, and 7 for CC, CT, and TT variants, respectively) was performed.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific sample sizes for the ex-vivo experiments by genotype.

claim: 250 patients were admitted to ICU due to suspected or confirmed COVID-19 during the study period.
source: About 250 patients were admitted in ICU due to suspected or confirmed COVID-19.
evidence: The manuscript states the total number of patients screened for the study.

claim: The genotyping distribution was 53 CC, 110 CT, and 64 TT for IFIH1 rs1990760 variants.
source: IFIH1 rs1990760 variants in this population met Hardy-Weinberg conditions (53 CC, 110 CT, 64 TT, chi-square p=0.19).
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific genotype counts.

claim: Ingenuity pathway analysis revealed several gene networks involved in regulation of inflammatory response among differentially expressed genes.
source: Ingenuity pathway analysis revealed several gene networks involved in the regulation of the inflammatory response among the differentially expressed genes (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes pathway analysis results with reference to figures.

claim: Visual inspection of the heatmap reveals that differences in gene expression are quantitative rather than qualitative.
source: Visual inspection of the heatmap reveals that differences are quantitative rather than qualitative.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the heatmap data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The absence of differences in viral clearance and the late increase in IL-6 suggest that worse outcome is more related to disruption of immunoregulatory mechanisms than to antiviral responses.
source: The absence of differences in viral clearance and the late increase in IL-6 in these patients suggest that this worse outcome is more related to the disruption of ongoing immunoregulatory mechanisms than to antiviral responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the viral clearance and IL-6 data.

claim: The ex-vivo experiments do not fully elucidate the molecular mechanisms behind the interaction between TT variants and steroids.
source: Our ex-vivo experiments do not fully elucidate the molecular mechanisms behind the interaction between TT variants and steroids, as the effects of FOXO3 upregulation and IL6 expression may be variable (Joseph et al., 2016), but clearly illustrate that this specific combination may disrupt the ongoing self-regulation of inflammation.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges limitations of the ex-vivo experiments while drawing conclusions.

claim: The findings point toward the therapeutic potential of MDA5 modulation in COVID-19.
source: Our findings point toward the therapeutic potential of MDA5 modulation in COVID-19, either induced by steroids or targeted by other drugs.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: Amelioration of MDA5-dependent RNA sensing could avoid exacerbated inflammatory response without impairing viral clearance.
source: Amelioration of MDA5-dependent RNA sensing could avoid an exacerbated inflammatory response without impairing viral clearance.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic hypothesis based on the study findings.

claim: The interferon response triggered by MDA5 is unable to control viral replication.
source: In this sense, it has been described that the interferon response triggered by MDA5 is unable to control viral replication (Rebendenne et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this statement.

claim: Genetic ablation of IFIH1 results in increased viral loads and decreased cytokine production.
source: However, genetic ablation of IFIH1 results in increased viral loads and decreased cytokine production (Yin et al., 2021), so this approach must be viewed with caution.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference supporting this statement and draws a cautionary conclusion.

claim: Steroids may decrease mortality in an unselected ARDS population.
source: Steroids may decrease mortality in an unselected ARDS population (Villar et al., 2020), but the role of underlying genotypes has not been addressed.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference for steroid efficacy in ARDS and notes a knowledge gap.

claim: An experimental model of Coxsackie virus infection revealed lower IFIH1 and CXCL10 expression in cells with the TT variant with no relevant differences in viral clearance.
source: An experimental model of Coxsackie virus infection revealed lower IFIH1 and CXCL10 expression in cells with the TT variant (Domsgen et al., 2016), with no relevant differences in viral clearance.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing findings in an experimental model.

claim: Total absence of MDA5 results in impaired clearance of West Nile virus.
source: However, total absence of MDA5 results in impaired clearance of West Nile virus (Errett et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference describing findings for West Nile virus.

claim: Steroid treatment was not randomized in the study.
source: Second, steroid treatment was not randomized, so we cannot discard other underlying factors responsible for the observed differences.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this as a limitation of the study design.

claim: There were no baseline differences among treatment groups suggesting higher severity in steroid-treated patients.
source: Although there could be confounding by indication, there were no baseline differences among groups suggesting a higher severity in steroid-treated patients.
evidence: The manuscript addresses potential confounding by examining baseline characteristics.

claim: The sample is representative of European population with limited racial diversity.
source: In addition, our sample is representative of European population with a limited racial diversity that may have influenced our results, as the in-silico analyses further suggest.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this as a limitation affecting generalizability.

claim: No genetic markers have been associated with mortality in cohorts of infected COVID-19 patients prior to this study.
source: However, no genetic markers have been associated to mortality in cohorts of infected patients.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts this study with previous genetic studies focused on susceptibility rather than outcome.

claim: According to the study data, rs1990760 is linked to outcome, but no inferences on susceptibility to severe COVID-19 can be extracted.
source: According to our data, rs1990760 is linked to the outcome, but no inferences on susceptibility to severe COVID-19 can be extracted.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the scope and limitations of the findings.

claim: The systemic response to severe COVID-19 is regulated by genetic factors that modulate the response to infection and prescribed therapy.
source: These findings suggest that the systemic response to severe COVID-19 is regulated by genetic factors that modulate the response to the infection and the prescribed therapy and, ultimately, may impact the outcome.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the study findings.

claim: COVID-19 populations with a low proportion of the rs1990760 TT variant would show a better response to dexamethasone.
source: These findings may support the hypothesis that COVID-19 populations with a low proportion of the rs1990760 TT variant would show a better response to dexamethasone.
evidence: This is a hypothesis generated from the study findings and in-silico simulations.

claim: The impact of treatment with steroids along a given population may depend on intrinsic individual characteristics, allowing a personalized approach based on a specific genomic biomarker.
source: According to our results, the impact of the treatment with steroids along a given population may depend on intrinsic individual characteristics, allowing a personalized approach based on a specific genomic biomarker.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study findings regarding personalized medicine.

claim: Any population enriched for patients with CC/CT variants in rs1990760 will show higher mortality rates and a better response to steroids, due to the low proportion of TT variants.
source: Indeed, as shown by the in-silico trials, any population enriched for patients with CC/CT variants in rs1990760 will show higher mortality rates and a better response to steroids, due to the low proportion of TT variants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in-silico simulation results.

claim: No other genomic markers of personalized therapies in critically ill patients have been identified to date.
source: To date, no other genomic markers of personalized therapies in critically ill patients have been identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.
